set.stem: A 22-year-old woman with asthma has had wheeze and breathlessness for 6 hours despite using her salbutamol inhaler several times. HR 128/min, RR 30/min, SpO2 89% on air; peak flow 40% of predicted. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: An SpO2 below 92% is a life-threatening feature (BTS/SIGN), even though a PEF of 40% on its own would only grade the attack as acute severe (33–50%). Alongside oxygen to SpO2 94–98% and prednisolone 40–50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone), she needs oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 0.5 mg and a single IV dose of magnesium sulfate 1.2–2 g over 20 minutes, with early senior and ICU review. High-dose ICS and LAMAs are maintenance treatments, oral prednisolone alone leaves the bronchospasm untreated, and discharge would be dangerous.

set.stem: A 35-year-old man with asthma has had worsening breathlessness and chest tightness for 1 day with night-time cough, and has used his reliever 8 times in 24 hours. HR 118/min, RR 32/min, BP 128/74 mmHg, SpO2 93% on air; there is diffuse wheeze with accessory muscle use. PEF is 45% of predicted and a chest X-ray shows no pneumonia. What is the next best step?
set.explanation: PEF 33–50%, RR ≥25/min and HR ≥110/min define acute severe asthma; with SpO2 still ≥92% and no exhaustion or silent chest there is no life-threatening feature. First-line treatment is repeated high-dose nebulised (or spacer) salbutamol, with ipratropium if the response is poor, oxygen if SpO2 falls below 94%, and an early systemic corticosteroid (prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for at least 5 days). IV magnesium is reserved for a poor response to initial bronchodilators or life-threatening features, and maintenance changes (ICS–formoterol, LAMA, montelukast) are made once the attack is controlled, before discharge.

why: SpO2 90% met a life-threatening criterion (<92%), which would make IV magnesium defensible; SpO2 changed to 93% and PEF to 45% so the vignette is unambiguously acute severe asthma

set.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD has had 3 days of worsening breathlessness, cough with yellow sputum and wheeze. HR 108/min, RR 28/min, BP 138/84 mmHg, SpO2 87% on air. ABG on air: pH 7.32, PaCO2 7.7 kPa (58 mmHg), HCO3− 30 mmol/L, PaO2 7.7 kPa (58 mmHg). There is diffuse wheeze with prolonged expiration. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: This is an infective COPD exacerbation with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic acidosis (pH 7.32, PaCO2 7.7 kPa, raised bicarbonate). Immediate treatment is controlled oxygen via a 24–28% Venturi mask to SpO2 88–92%, nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium, prednisolone 30–40 mg for 5 days and an antibiotic for purulent sputum (amoxicillin, doxycycline or clarithromycin); if pH <7.35 and PaCO2 >6.5 kPa persist after about an hour of optimal therapy, start NIV. LTOT is assessed only when stable, and ICS/LABA, montelukast and roflumilast are not acute treatments.

set.stem: A 72-year-old man with advanced COPD is reviewed when clinically stable, 5 weeks after his last exacerbation. ABG on air: PaO2 7.5 kPa (56 mmHg), PaCO2 6.9 kPa (52 mmHg); SpO2 89%. He has mild ankle oedema and echocardiography shows pulmonary hypertension. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: LTOT (at least 15 hours a day) is indicated in stable COPD when PaO2 is <7.3 kPa, or 7.3–8.0 kPa with secondary polycythaemia, peripheral oedema or pulmonary hypertension (NICE NG115; two ABGs at least 3 weeks apart). His PaO2 of 7.5 kPa with oedema and pulmonary hypertension qualifies, and LTOT improves survival (MRC and NOTT trials). Nocturnal oxygen alone gives no survival benefit, more bronchodilator does not correct hypoxaemia, acetazolamide is not a treatment and waiting 3 months only delays therapy; he must not smoke because of the fire risk.

Wheeze is generated by airflow through narrowed airways: bronchospasm in asthma, inflammation and secretions in acute bronchitis, and a localised (often monophonic) wheeze distal to an inhaled foreign body. A pneumothorax causes sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness with reduced breath sounds and hyper-resonance, not wheeze. Remember that not all wheeze is asthma: also consider COPD, left ventricular failure ('cardiac asthma') and large-airway obstruction (stridor).

why: Same question as airway-0005 (wheeze with dyspnoea — pneumothorax is the exception)

set.explanation: Smoking cessation (which slows the decline in FEV1) and long-term oxygen therapy in chronic resting hypoxaemia (PaO2 <7.3 kPa, or <8 kPa with cor pulmonale or polycythaemia) are the classic interventions that prolong survival in COPD. GOLD 2025 also credits pulmonary rehabilitation after hospitalisation, home NIV for persistent hypercapnia, triple ICS/LABA/LAMA therapy in frequent exacerbators and lung volume reduction in selected patients. LABA/ICS dual therapy did not significantly reduce mortality (TORCH), repeated steroid courses cause harm, and weight reduction is not a survival measure (low BMI is itself a poor prognostic sign).

why: Same question as airway-0006 (survival in COPD — smoking cessation plus LTOT)
Same idea and level as airway-0006 (which interventions improve prognosis in COPD)

set.stem: A 65-year-old man has had cough and sputum for 4 years and has been diagnosed with COPD. Which test can differentiate chronic bronchitis from emphysema?
set.explanation: DLCO (TLCO) reflects the area of functioning alveolar–capillary membrane. In emphysema, destruction of alveolar walls reduces DLCO and KCO, whereas in predominant chronic bronchitis the airways are diseased but the gas-exchange surface is preserved, so DLCO is near normal. Spirometry and peak flow show obstruction in both, and the chest X-ray is insensitive; CT is the imaging test that demonstrates emphysema.

BTS/SIGN life-threatening features are PEF <33% of best or predicted, SpO2 <92%, PaO2 <8 kPa, a 'normal' PaCO2 (4.6–6.0 kPa), silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, arrhythmia, exhaustion, altered consciousness and hypotension. PEF 33–50%, RR ≥25/min, HR ≥110/min and inability to complete sentences in one breath indicate acute severe (not life-threatening) asthma, and a respiratory rate of 22/min is not a severity marker.

Asthma can start at any age, may be seasonal (pollens) or perennial (house-dust mite, animal dander), is characteristically variable with symptom-free intervals, and nocturnal cough and wheeze are typical. In childhood it is more common in boys, but after puberty the ratio reverses, so adult asthma is more common and tends to be more severe in women. The false statement is therefore that it is more common and more severe in adult men.

why: Same question as airway-0009 (asthma is not more common or severe in adult men)
Same idea as airway-0009 (asthma is not more severe in adult men than women)

set.stem: A patient with long-standing chronic bronchitis presents with increased cough, sputum and severe breathlessness. ABG on air: PaO2 8.2 kPa, PaCO2 8.6 kPa, pH 7.20. Which of the following should be avoided?
set.explanation: This is acute hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure in COPD. His PaO2 of 8.2 kPa (SpO2 about 90%) is already within the target of 88–92%, and higher concentrations such as 35% worsen hypercapnia, mainly by releasing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worsening V/Q mismatch) and by the Haldane effect, with loss of hypoxic drive playing a smaller part. Oxygen should be controlled (24–28% Venturi) and titrated to 88–92%. Nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, prednisolone 30–40 mg for 5 days and NIV (for pH <7.35 with PaCO2 >6.5 kPa persisting despite medical therapy) are all indicated.

why: PaCO2 6.6 kPa cannot produce pH 7.20 as described (likely OCR of 8.6); ABG made consistent, 'contraindicated' reworded to 'should be avoided', options clarified and NIV added as a distractor

set.explanation: Indications for intubation and mechanical ventilation in acute asthma are exhaustion, drowsiness, confusion or coma, respiratory arrest, and worsening hypoxaemia or a rising PaCO2 with acidosis despite maximal therapy. Inability to speak more than a few words, PEF 33–50% and tachypnoea mark acute severe asthma that needs intensive treatment but not, by themselves, ventilation. NIV is not a routine alternative in acute asthma; involve ICU early so that intubation is performed by an experienced anaesthetist.

Chest X-ray signs of COPD (hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, bullae, attenuated peripheral vessels) correlate poorly with the degree of airflow limitation, which is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1 (GOLD 1–4). Lung volumes (TLC, RV, FRC) quantify hyperinflation and gas trapping, and body plethysmography is preferred when there are bullae because helium dilution underestimates volumes in poorly ventilated spaces. A low peak flow shows obstruction but cannot distinguish COPD from asthma or other causes.

why: Same question as airway-0012 (COPD — radiographic signs do not correlate with airflow limitation)

set.explanation: Long-acting bronchodilators — a LAMA such as tiotropium and a LABA such as salmeterol or formoterol — not short-acting ones, are the maintenance treatment of moderate to severe COPD; GOLD 2025 recommends a LABA+LAMA combination for most symptomatic patients, with short-acting agents kept for relief. The inhaled route delivers drug to the airway with fewer systemic effects, and breathlessness often improves through reduced hyperinflation even when FEV1 barely changes. Once-daily tiotropium outperforms four-times-daily ipratropium for exacerbations and quality of life.

set.stem: A patient with asthma using a regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus an as-needed short-acting beta2-agonist wakes at night with cough and occasional wheeze three to four times a week. Inhaler technique and adherence are good. What is the best next step?
options: Switch to low-dose ICS–formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
set.explanation: Night waking several times a week on low-dose ICS plus SABA means uncontrolled asthma. After checking adherence, technique and triggers, BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 and GINA 2024 recommend switching to low-dose ICS–formoterol MART (e.g. budesonide–formoterol), which adds a LABA to the ICS and uses the same inhaler as reliever, reducing severe exacerbations compared with fixed-dose ICS/LABA plus SABA. A leukotriene receptor antagonist is now a later add-on if asthma remains uncontrolled on MART, theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, and maintenance oral steroids are a last resort in specialist-managed severe asthma. A LABA must never be used without an ICS.

why: Option 'long-acting beta2-agonist' updated to ICS–formoterol MART, the current BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 and GINA 2024 step-up; stem now states low-dose ICS with good adherence
Same idea and level as airway-0014 (asthma uncontrolled on low-dose ICS plus SABA — next step-up, now ICS–formoterol MART)

set.stem: A 54-year-old smoker has cough, sputum and breathlessness. There is vesicular breathing with a prolonged expiratory phase, low-pitched expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles throughout the chest. Spirometry: FEV1/VC 56%, rising to 68% after bronchodilator; post-bronchodilator FEV1 62% of predicted. What is the diagnosis?
set.explanation: A post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (or FEV1/VC) below 0.70 in a symptomatic smoker confirms persistent airflow limitation, i.e. COPD (GOLD 2025). Partial reversibility, as here, does not exclude COPD, whereas in asthma the ratio typically normalises after bronchodilator. Coarse crackles reflect airway secretions of chronic bronchitis; extrinsic allergic alveolitis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis cause a restrictive pattern with a normal or high FEV1/FVC and fine inspiratory crackles.

set.stem: A 54-year-old smoker has cough, sputum and breathlessness. There is vesicular breathing with a prolonged expiratory phase, low-pitched expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles throughout the chest. Spirometry: FEV1/VC 56%, rising to 68% after bronchodilator; post-bronchodilator FEV1 62% of predicted. According to the spirometric classification of severity based on post-bronchodilator FEV1, he has:
set.explanation: COPD is diagnosed by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70, and the airflow limitation is then graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted (GOLD 2025): GOLD 1 mild ≥80%, GOLD 2 moderate 50–79%, GOLD 3 severe 30–49% and GOLD 4 very severe <30%. An FEV1 of 62% predicted is GOLD 2, moderate. GOLD combines this grade with symptoms (mMRC or CAT) and exacerbation history (groups A, B and E) to choose treatment.

why: Stem omitted the FEV1 % predicted needed to grade severity; post-bronchodilator FEV1 62% of predicted added (GOLD 2, moderate)

set.stem: A 54-year-old smoker has cough, sputum and breathlessness. There is vesicular breathing with a prolonged expiratory phase, low-pitched expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles throughout the chest. Spirometry: FEV1/VC 56%, rising to 68% after bronchodilator; post-bronchodilator FEV1 62% of predicted. What is the most important step in his management?
set.explanation: Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention in a smoker with COPD: it is the only measure shown to slow the accelerated decline in FEV1 (Lung Health Study) and it improves survival. Offer behavioural support with pharmacotherapy (varenicline, nicotine replacement or bupropion) at every contact. Short- and long-acting bronchodilators, including ipratropium, relieve symptoms and reduce exacerbations but do not modify disease progression.

set.stem: A 54-year-old smoker has cough, sputum and breathlessness. There is vesicular breathing with a prolonged expiratory phase, low-pitched expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles throughout the chest. Spirometry: FEV1/VC 56%, rising to 68% after bronchodilator; post-bronchodilator FEV1 62% of predicted. Which of the following statements about the treatment of his disease is NOT true?
set.explanation: Maintenance oral corticosteroids are not recommended in COPD: they give no sustained benefit and cause myopathy, osteoporosis, diabetes and infection, so systemic steroids are used only as short courses (prednisolone 30–40 mg for 5 days) for exacerbations. Roflumilast, a PDE4 inhibitor, modestly improves FEV1 and reduces moderate and severe exacerbations in patients with FEV1 <50% and chronic bronchitis, and long-term azithromycin (250 mg daily or 500 mg three times weekly) reduces exacerbations. Pneumococcal, annual influenza, COVID-19 and RSV vaccination are recommended (GOLD 2025).

set.stem: A 54-year-old smoker has cough, sputum and breathlessness. There is vesicular breathing with a prolonged expiratory phase, low-pitched expiratory wheezes and coarse crackles throughout the chest. Spirometry: FEV1/VC 56%, rising to 68% after bronchodilator; post-bronchodilator FEV1 62% of predicted. Which of the following is NOT a complication of his disease?
set.explanation: COPD itself does not cause finger clubbing; clubbing in a patient with COPD should prompt a search for lung cancer, bronchiectasis or pulmonary fibrosis. Chronic hypoxaemia causes secondary polycythaemia and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, leading to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale (right heart failure), while ruptured bullae cause secondary pneumothorax. COPD can produce either type 1 or type 2 respiratory failure.

why: Type 1 respiratory failure does occur in COPD (hypoxaemia without hypercapnia, e.g. emphysema), so the key was indefensible; distractor replaced by finger clubbing, which COPD does not cause

set.stem: All of the following are characteristic of asthma EXCEPT:
options: It is rare before 5 years of age
It can be seasonal or perennial
It can start at any age
The patient can be completely free of symptoms between episodes
set.explanation: Asthma frequently begins in early childhood — most children with persistent asthma have symptoms before 5 years of age, although the diagnosis is clinical at that age because spirometry is difficult. It can start at any age (including late-onset, often non-atopic, asthma), may be seasonal or perennial depending on the trigger, and its hallmark is variability, so patients can be symptom-free between episodes.

set.stem: A 53-year-old woman with a 30-year history of asthma has worsening control despite maximal inhaled therapy, a chronic cough productive of green sputum, breathlessness and wheeze. A CT scan of her chest is shown. What does it show?
set.explanation: The CT shows dilated, thick-walled proximal bronchi in the upper lobes, wider than their accompanying arteries (signet ring sign) — bronchiectasis. Central upper-lobe bronchiectasis in a long-standing asthmatic with deteriorating control strongly suggests allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA): check total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG and eosinophils, and treat with oral prednisolone with or without itraconazole. Emphysema appears as low-attenuation areas without walls, and honeycombing is basal and subpleural; typical asthma shows only mild wall thickening or air trapping.

why: Parse fragment: first half of the stem of airway-0026 (question rejoined there)

set.stem: A 37-year-old woman with asthma has difficult asthma control that worsens every April and May. Serum allergy testing shows: total IgE 1241 kU/L; specific IgE to dog 24 kU/L, cat 4 kU/L, tree pollen 0.2 kU/L, oilseed rape 34 kU/L and grass pollen 25 kU/L. What is the most likely explanation for her presentation?
options: She has exercise-induced asthma, so IgE testing is irrelevant
She has concealed exposure to animals, as dog and cat specific IgE are raised
She is non-adherent to medication, as total IgE remains high
She is sensitised to montelukast, and the IgE results represent cross-reactivity
Her asthma is triggered by seasonal pollens (oilseed rape and grass)
set.explanation: The pattern of deterioration each April–May, together with strong sensitisation to oilseed rape (which flowers in spring) and grass pollen, points to seasonal allergic asthma. Specific IgE shows sensitisation, which is clinically relevant only when it matches the history, so the dog and cat results do not explain a seasonal pattern, and total IgE is not a marker of adherence. Optimise ICS-containing treatment before the pollen season, treat coexisting allergic rhinitis and reduce exposure.

why: Stem rejoined from two parse fragments (airway-0025 and this item); key set to seasonal pollen sensitisation

set.stem: A 45-year-old smoker with cough, wheeze and productive sputum undergoes pulmonary function testing. Pre-bronchodilator: FEV1 2.6 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.59. Post-bronchodilator: FEV1 3.2 L, FVC 4.4 L, FEV1/FVC 0.73. What does the testing show?
set.explanation: The FEV1/FVC of 0.59 shows obstruction; after bronchodilator FEV1 rises by 600 mL (23%) and the ratio normalises to 0.73. An increase of ≥12% and ≥200 mL is significant reversibility, and a gain of ≥400 mL with normalisation of the ratio strongly favours asthma over COPD despite the smoking history. A restrictive defect would reduce FVC with a normal or high ratio, and salbutamol is the agent used to test reversibility, not a confounder.

set.stem: A 27-year-old woman with severe atopic asthma, who is 26 weeks pregnant, presents with worsening nocturnal cough and breathlessness. PEF is 240 L/min (best 450 L/min). Her medications are high-dose ICS/LABA, oral montelukast and an as-needed SABA. What should be the next step in her management?
set.explanation: A PEF of 240 L/min against a best of 450 L/min (53%) with worsening nocturnal symptoms is an exacerbation needing a systemic corticosteroid: prednisolone 40–50 mg daily for at least 5 days. Uncontrolled asthma and maternal hypoxaemia are far more dangerous to the fetus than steroids, and ICS, LABA, montelukast and SABA should all be continued in pregnancy. Stepping down treatment, stopping montelukast or giving antibiotics without evidence of infection are wrong, and LMWH treats VTE, not asthma.

set.stem: A 48-year-old man with asthma has increasingly frequent exacerbations, nocturnal cough and blood eosinophilia. He uses fluticasone–salmeterol twice daily (good adherence and technique) and salbutamol as required, and has just started a 5-day course of prednisolone for the current exacerbation. According to current BTS/NICE/SIGN guidance, what is the most appropriate change to his maintenance therapy?
options: Switch to budesonide–formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
set.explanation: Asthma that remains uncontrolled with exacerbations on fixed-dose ICS/LABA plus a SABA should be switched to ICS–formoterol MART (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024, GINA 2024), which reduces severe exacerbations because every reliever dose also delivers ICS. If he is still uncontrolled on moderate-dose MART, raised blood eosinophils or FeNO should prompt specialist referral for a biologic (anti-IL-5/5R, anti-IL-4R, anti-TSLP, or anti-IgE if allergic); a trial of montelukast or a LAMA is suggested mainly when type 2 markers are not raised. Home nebulisers can mask deterioration, and antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of bacterial infection.

why: Source key (add montelukast, older BTS guidance) is outdated; BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 and GINA 2024 recommend switching to ICS–formoterol MART, so options and key updated

set.stem: A 43-year-old woman who smokes and works in a bakery presents with cough, breathlessness and wheeze, which deteriorate after 3 weeks back at work. Which test is most helpful to assess for occupational asthma?
set.explanation: Serial PEF recordings — at least four times a day for 3–4 weeks, covering periods at work and away from work — are the first-line objective test for occupational asthma because they show work-related variability. Specific IgE or skin-prick testing to flour or amylase shows sensitisation but does not prove that work causes her asthma, and histamine challenge, reversibility testing and sputum eosinophils support asthma without linking it to the workplace. Confirmed cases need early removal from exposure.

Atopy — the genetic predisposition to produce IgE against common environmental allergens, shown by positive skin-prick tests — is the strongest identifiable risk factor for asthma. Maternal smoking, air pollution, diet and respiratory viral infections contribute to the development or exacerbation of asthma but are weaker risk factors.

Asthma severity tends to remain relatively constant within an individual: mild asthma rarely progresses to severe disease, and severe asthma is usually severe from onset, even though control fluctuates. Diagnosis rests on symptoms plus objective tests (FeNO, spirometry with reversibility, PEF variability), with bronchial challenge only when these are inconclusive. Prevalence rose markedly over recent decades, mortality has fallen with ICS use, and atopy is the major risk factor.

Fatal asthma is an airway disease: mucus plugs occlude the bronchi, the mucosa is infiltrated by eosinophils, mast cells and activated Th2 lymphocytes, the wall is oedematous with smooth-muscle hypertrophy, and subepithelial collagen deposition thickens the basement membrane (remodelling). The alveoli are typically spared, so alveolar infiltration by eosinophils and neutrophils is not expected; it would suggest eosinophilic pneumonia or infection.

options: A 24-year-old with cough and wheeze for 6 weeks after a viral respiratory infection
A 26-year-old with cough and occasional wheeze when exercising in cold weather
A 34-year-old with chronic cough whose FEV1 increases from 1.68 L to 1.98 L (18%) after salbutamol
A 44-year-old laboratory worker who handles mice and has cough and wheeze towards the end of each working week
A 60-year-old heavy smoker with chronic breathlessness and airway hyperreactivity
set.explanation: Asthma requires compatible symptoms plus objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction; an FEV1 rise of ≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator (here 300 mL, 18%) confirms reversibility. Post-viral cough and wheeze usually reflect transient airway hyperresponsiveness, cold-air or exercise symptoms need objective confirmation, suspected occupational asthma needs serial PEF, and a heavy smoker with chronic breathlessness most likely has COPD — airway hyperreactivity alone does not make the diagnosis.

set.stem: A 24-year-old woman with mild asthma uses her salbutamol inhaler 4–7 times a week and takes no other treatment. What do you advise?
set.explanation: SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended (GINA 2024, BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024) because it leaves airway inflammation untreated and is linked to severe exacerbations and asthma deaths. For mild asthma, as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (anti-inflammatory reliever, AIR) reduces severe exacerbations by about two-thirds compared with SABA alone; regular low-dose ICS plus SABA is the alternative, and MART is used when symptoms are frequent or nocturnal. LABA monotherapy (salmeterol) increases asthma deaths, tiotropium is a later add-on, and montelukast is less effective than ICS.

why: Joke option (goldfish) replaced; 'add beclometasone' updated to as-needed ICS–formoterol because SABA-only treatment is no longer recommended (GINA 2024, BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024)
Same idea and level as airway-0035 (asthma uncontrolled on SABA alone — start ICS-containing treatment)

set.stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with mild persistent asthma is well controlled on an inhaled corticosteroid and salbutamol as needed. Which statement is correct?
set.explanation: Asthma in pregnancy follows a 'rule of thirds' — roughly a third improve, a third worsen and a third are unchanged — so neither a >70% chance of improvement nor of worsening is correct. Inhaled corticosteroids, SABAs, LABAs and montelukast are safe in pregnancy and should be continued, because poorly controlled asthma with maternal hypoxaemia is the real risk to the fetus; control should be monitored. Tiotropium is not a reliever, and salmeterol must never replace an ICS.

set.stem: A 34-year-old man with severe persistent asthma expectorates brown mucus plugs and has marked blood eosinophilia. Which test is indicated next?
set.explanation: Brown mucus plugs, eosinophilia and poorly controlled asthma suggest allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The key screening test is total serum IgE (typically >500 IU/mL, often >1000) with Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE or skin-prick testing; Aspergillus IgG and HRCT (central bronchiectasis, mucus plugging) then support the diagnosis. Sweat chloride and nasal nitric oxide are tests for cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia, and aspirin desensitisation is for aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease. Treatment is oral prednisolone with or without itraconazole.

why: Same idea and level as airway-0002 (acute severe asthma — first step is nebulised salbutamol with steroid)

set.explanation: A silent chest means airflow is so reduced that too little air moves to generate wheeze; it is a life-threatening feature (with SpO2 <92%, PEF <33%, cyanosis, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, confusion and a normal or rising PaCO2) and signals impending respiratory failure. Tachycardia and tachypnoea are features of acute severe asthma, and louder wheeze shows that air is still moving. She needs oxygen, nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium, steroids, IV magnesium and urgent ICU review.

options: Reduced FEV1 and reduced FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FEV1 and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC and normal FEV1:FVC ratio
Reduced FVC and increased FEV1:FVC ratio
set.explanation: Asthma is an obstructive disorder: bronchoconstriction reduces FEV1 proportionally more than FVC, so the FEV1:FVC ratio falls below 0.70 (or the lower limit of normal), and the obstruction is typically reversible (≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator). A reduced FVC with a normal or increased ratio indicates restriction, as in interstitial lung disease or neuromuscular and chest wall disease. During an acute attack, PEF or FEV1 is the practical bedside measure of severity.

An inspiratory fall in systolic BP of up to 10 mmHg is normal, so a pulsus paradoxus of 5 mmHg predicts a benign course, whereas values above about 25 mmHg indicate severe obstruction. Silent chest, hypercapnia, thoracoabdominal paradox (diaphragmatic fatigue) and altered mental status are signs of life-threatening or near-fatal asthma that warrant ICU and possible intubation — especially in someone previously intubated, a major risk factor for fatal asthma.

set.stem: A 30-year-old athlete presents with intermittent wheezing that begins shortly after running. He smokes 20–40 cigarettes a day and has done so for 5 years. Which finding would be consistent with asthma?
set.explanation: Wheeze after exercise suggests exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or asthma, whose defining feature is variable, reversible obstruction — an FEV1 rise of ≥12% and ≥200 mL after bronchodilator (or a fall after exercise challenge). Heavy smoking raises the possibility of early COPD, in which reversibility is usually limited. Hyperinflation can occur in both, hypoxaemia is not expected between attacks, a reduced FVC suggests restriction, and orthopnoea points to heart failure or diaphragm weakness.

set.stem: A 28-year-old builder attends the respiratory clinic with a 6-month history of progressive exertional breathlessness and cough. His GP started a salbutamol inhaler, which he now uses several times a day. He has smoked since the age of 18 (10 pack-years) and reports occupational exposure to asbestos. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.68; FEV1 is 3.0 L before and 3.4 L after bronchodilator. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) and long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) inhaler
Low-dose ICS–formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)
set.explanation: A young man with only 10 pack-years, obstruction (FEV1/FVC 0.68) and a 400 mL bronchodilator response most likely has asthma; an FEV1 improvement of ≥400 mL strongly suggests asthma rather than COPD, and asbestos causes pleural disease or restriction, not obstruction. Using a SABA several times a day means he needs ICS-containing treatment, and BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024 recommends low-dose ICS–formoterol MART for a newly diagnosed adult with frequent symptoms. LABA+LAMA is COPD treatment, a LABA without ICS is dangerous in asthma, and omalizumab and oral steroids are reserved for severe asthma; he must also stop smoking.

why: Source key (LABA+LAMA) contradicts the data and the source's own explanation: 400 mL reversibility in a young man with 10 pack-years indicates asthma, so ICS-containing therapy (updated to low-dose ICS–formoterol MART) is correct
